summary.text: An 81-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, dyslipidaemia, osteoporosis, anxiety and gastrooesophageal reflux disease, whose listed medications were irbesartan, hydrochlorothiazide, thyroxine, rosuvastatin, sertraline, aspirin and metoprolol, presented to a peripheral emergency department with a two-week history of shortness of breath. She had been commenced on oral antibiotics for a lower respiratory tract infection in the community. She denied chest pain.

In the emergency department she was in complete heart block with a ventricular escape of 48 bpm. High sensitivity troponin and BNP were elevated, a respiratory viral PCR swab returned positive for picornavirus, and she was transported to a tertiary hospital. Echocardiogram showed apical hypokinesis; catheterisation on day 9 showed nonobstructive coronary disease, a focal 50% mid left circumflex stenosis and near normalisation of the apical hypokinesis. Takotsubo syndrome was diagnosed; cardiac MRI and biopsy were not pursued.

Complete heart block continued after metoprolol was stopped. She was initially managed conservatively and the picornavirus infection was managed conservatively; nine days after presentation, once able to lie flat, a dual chamber Biotronik pacemaker was implanted. She was discharged on aspirin, irbesartan, rosuvastatin and sertraline.

Pacemaker interrogation 6 weeks after implantation showed underlying complete heart block with 100% ventricular pacing, no tachyarrhythmias and satisfactory device parameters. She remained independent in the community 6 months following discharge.

ambiguities.issue: The discussion says the Takotsubo syndrome appears to have been precipitated by the lower respiratory tract infection with picornavirus; this is the authors' hedged inference.

ambiguities.issue: The authors state it is unclear when complete heart block developed and that the possibility of progressive conduction disease is high; the order of Takotsubo syndrome and heart block is not established.
